world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: 2.3 Stress. Stress is not contrastive. In two or three syllable words stress falls on the penultimate vowel except when the word final syllable is heavier than the penultimate, i.e. the final syllable has more segments than the previous syllable, in which case stress is on the final syllable; compare: (5) ma»ma.sa 'good'; la»rai 'grate'. In words of four or more syllables, secondary stress falls on each alternate syllable to the right of the final stressed syllable, except when the following syllable is heavier. (6) «a.bu«a.bu»ka.ra 'quick'; ma«nai.la»rai 'pudding'; ma«tai»ma.sa 'sun'. [p. 9] ... Stress falls predicably on penultimate syllable. [p. 8]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is non-contrastive and falls on the penultimate syllable, unless the final syllable is heavier (has more segments, e.g. a diphthong or a closed syllable) than the penult, in which case it falls on the final syllable. In words of four or more syllables secondary stresses fall on alternating syllables leftward of the primary stress (the author's 'to the right of the final stressed syllable' refers to his notation), again blocked when the adjacent syllable is heavier. The chapter opening summarises this as predictably penultimate stress. Vowel-deletion morphophonemics apply before stress assignment (section 2.4).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: in words of four or more syllables secondary stress on each alternate syllable away from the primary-stressed syllable, except when the following syllable is heavier (examples,a.bu,a.bu'ka.ra 'quick', ma,nai.la'rai 'pudding', ma,tai'ma.sa 'sun').
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress when the final syllable is heavier than the penult (la'rai 'grate'); the two morphophonemic vowel-deletion rules (CV.CV[high]+alveolar C -> CVC.C; V1#V1 -> V1) apply before stress assignment, so surface clusters do not disturb the rule. Author also notes (p. 8) that Tiale speakers pronounce high vowels where Merei has consonant clusters (tlui ~ tului 'pull'), so syllable counts can differ between the two varieties.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress, stated on isolated lexical words with diacritics in examples; no discussion of phrase-level stress or citation-form effects. The description is of Merei, the author's wife's variety, in the villages Angoru, Navele, Tombet, Vusvogo.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Merei (Glottolog mere1242, ISO lmb; = Tryon 1976 'Lametin' list 47), not Tiale directly. Tiale (tial1239, ISO mnl) = Tryon 1976 'Malmariv' list 44 (Lynch & Crowley 2001:54). Lynch & Crowley 2001 treat Merei-Tiale as one language and Chung 2005:3 reports 90-93% cognacy and mutual intelligibility by recorded text test ('they might be considered varieties of one language', citing Stahl 1996); Glottolog lists Malmariv/Tiale as alternate names under both mere1242 and tial1239. Chung 2005:8 notes one segmental difference (Tiale retains high vowels where Merei has clusters, tlui ~ tului), which can change syllable counts but no separate stress statement for Tiale exists. If the catalog keeps mere1242 and tial1239 apart, this entry should be filed as Merei with Tiale inheriting it by identity, and flagged as such.
